title: Back to Basics: The Why and How of Cannabis Legalization. Questions and Answers

content_html_sanitized:
When I first got involved in the “Marijuana Reform” movement, in 1972, almost all that I knew was that marijuana was less dangerous than alcohol, about which I knew too much, and that alcohol prohibition had been a disaster, and that almost no one was arrested for alcohol possession.

When I found out that people’s lives were being ruined by being arrested, my libertarian instincts kicked in and here I am, 30 million arrests later, and we are still adding over 200,000 more every year. Frankly, I am getting impatient. (And older.)

The main reason for not arresting marijuana users is simply personal freedom. If eighteen year olds can go fight for freedom, they should be free to smoke a joint and/or drink a beer, and - again- by any measure, weed is far less dangerous than alcohol.

So, there really must be a truly compelling argument, not some sociological or criminological or psychological or cardiovascular theory about why someone might not live as long as they might otherwise, if they are free. So cannabis possession has to be “decriminalized.”

See Politicized Psychiatry and the Rehab Rackets

That was easy, but where is the cannabis supposed to come from?

Can they grow it themselves? Of course! But what if they don’t have a garden? Or if they are too sick to be able to grow it? Can they get someone to grow it for them? Of course, but can the growers grow it for more than one person? How many? Can they charge for it?

There is really no compelling reason that gardeners should not be able to grow as much cannabis as possible, with the same regulations that would apply to cabbage, and the price set by the market.

There really are thousands of talented gardeners who could make a living legally doing what they do best, but are barred by unreasonable laws.

See Let Artisanal Marijuana Growers Replace the Black Market With Home Grown

And The Decline and Fall of Humboldt Countyhttps://marijuananews.com/articles/the-decline-and-fall-of-humboldt-county/current

However, people living in big cities may not have easy access to gardeners, or “farmers markets”, so why can’t they get cannabis from a retailer? And shouldn’t the regulations be the same or even less restrictive than for alcohol retailers?

There should be clearly printed THC and other cannabinoid percentages on packaging, just as there are on bottles of alcohol.

If someone can sell alcohol legally at a store, or get someone to deliver it to your home, why wouldn’t that be acceptable for cannabis?

And if people can go to a bar and drink alcohol, why can’t they go to a cannabis social club and smoke cannabis with their friends?

See Two Years Since the End of the Pandemic, Cannabis Continues Replacing Alcohol Socially

And why should there be legal restrictions on the number of clubs, beyond what the market will support? Arbitrary restrictions are a source of graft, payoffs to politicians and corrupt police.

And then where is all this cannabis coming from? There are hundreds of millions of cannabis users around the world, so the volume is enormous. And how should it be taxed?

Even if the taxes are earmarked for worthy causes, higher taxes will create a competitive advantage for the black market.

Should it be left in the black market with fentanyl? Should the profits go to organized crime or terrorist groups?

On the other hand, a booming legal cannabis industry will create jobs and tax revenue from profits, plus gigs for musicians and easy audiences for comedians.

But how effective has cannabis prohibition been?

When “marihuana”, as it was spelled then, was banned under the Marihuana Tax act of 1937, almost no one even knew what it was.

Seventy one years later, in 2008, after millions of arrests, a government survey found that “35 million Americans were willing to tell government representatives that they had used marijuana in the past year.”

This was six years before Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize marijuana, so they had to get it from the black market. That was slightly more than ten percent of the population at that time.

In 2009,  34 years after cannabis was first sold over the counter in The Netherlands, “Among adults in the Netherlands, 5.4 percent used cannabis, compared with the European average of 6.8 percent, according to an annual report by the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction, using the latest available figures.” They still are.

See Dutch among lowest cannabis users in Europe-report

AndMarijuana and Martinis at the Movies: How Prohibition Is Counter Productive and Glamorouses What It Is Trying to Ban

 Where do we go to get our freedom back? Wherever.
